locator.heading: Herb Robert

source_text:
THE Herb Robert is held in great estimation by farmers, who use it in
diseases of their cattle.

_Descript._] It rises up with a reddish stalk two feet high, having
divers leaves thereon, upon very long and reddish foot-stalks, divided
at the ends into three or five divisions, each of them cut in on
the edges, which sometimes turn reddish. At the tops of the stalks
come forth divers flowers made of five leaves, much larger than the
Dove’s-foot, and of a more reddish colour; after which come black
heads, as in others. The root is small and thready, and smells, as the
whole plant, very strong, almost stinking.

_Place._] This grows frequently every where by the way-sides, upon
ditch banks and waste grounds wheresoever one goes.

_Time._] It flowers in June and July chiefly, and the seed is ripe
shortly after.

_Government and virtues._] It is under the dominion of Venus. Herb
Robert is commended not only against the stone, but to stay blood,
where or howsoever flowing, it speedily heals all green wounds, and
is effectual in old ulcers in the privy parts, or elsewhere. You may
persuade yourself this is true, and also conceive a good reason for it,
do but consider it is an herb of Venus, for all it hath a man’s name.

pubmed.title: Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities of Geranium robertianum L. decoctions.
pubmed.relevance_note: Supports traditional use for wounds and ulcers via demonstrated anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties in decoctions.

pubmed.title: Promising effect of Geranium robertianum L. leaves and Aloe vera gel powder on Aspirin(®)-induced gastric ulcers in Wistar rats: anxiolytic behavioural effect, antioxidant activity, and protective pathways.
pubmed.relevance_note: Confirms gastroprotective effects relevant to treating old ulcers and gastric issues in animal models.

pubmed.title: Neuroprotective effects of Geranium Robertianum L. Aqueous extract on the cellular Parkinson's disease model.
pubmed.relevance_note: Suggests potential neuroprotective mechanisms, though direct evidence for bleeding or stone uses is absent in current literature.

evidence.summary: Modern research supports the traditional use of Geranium robertianum for wounds and ulcers through documented antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. Evidence suggests gastroprotective potential relevant to ulcer treatment, while data on bleeding cessation or stone dissolution remains limited in current studies.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID: 28858365, 37184667) confirms antioxidant/anti-inflammatory properties and gastric ulcer protection in rats. No clinical data supports claims for stones, bleeding, or ulcers.
concordance.uncertainty: Human efficacy for historical claims is unproven; animal models suggest limited mechanistic plausibility only.
